short: A trust that owns rent-earning buildings like offices and malls; its units trade on the stock exchange and most of the rent goes to investors.
kid: Imagine lots of friends put their coins together to own a big toy shop. Other children pay a little to play there, and every friend gets some of those coins back.
detail: A real estate investment trust (REIT) pools investors' money to own completed, income-producing property, mainly offices, malls, warehouses and hotels, and must pay out most of its income. In India, REITs are governed by SEBI's REIT Regulations of 2014; under the rules as of 2025, at least 80% of assets must be completed, rent-generating property and at least 90% of net distributable cash flows must be paid out at least every six months. India's first REIT, Embassy Office Parks, listed in 2019. In the US, REITs date from 1960 and must distribute at least 90% of taxable income. REIT units trade like shares, so their prices move with interest rates, occupancy and rents. The common confusion: a unitholder owns a slice of the trust, not a particular floor or shop, and cannot ask for a building to be sold.
example: Say you buy 100 units of a hypothetical XYZ REIT at ₹400 each, investing ₹40,000. If it distributes ₹7 per unit every quarter, you receive ₹700 a quarter, or ₹2,800 a year, a distribution yield of 7% on your cost.

short: An Indian property trust, created by SEBI in 2024, through which investors jointly own one or a few smaller rent-earning buildings.
kid: Ten friends each put in some coins to own one small sweet shop together. When customers pay to sit and eat there, the friends split those coins.
detail: A small and medium REIT (SM REIT) is a lighter version of a REIT that SEBI added to its REIT Regulations in 2024. Under the rules as of 2025, an SM REIT scheme holds completed, rent-earning property worth between ₹50 crore and ₹500 crore, often a single office building or a few floors, and the minimum investment is ₹10 lakh. One SM REIT can run several schemes, each with its own assets and investors, and the units are listed on a stock exchange. The framework brought fractional ownership platforms, which had been selling slices of commercial buildings to wealthy investors with little oversight, under SEBI regulation; such platforms had to register as SM REIT managers. The common confusion: an SM REIT is not a diversified small-cap fund; it is concentrated in one or two buildings, so one tenant leaving can cut income sharply, and units trade thinly.
example: Say a hypothetical SM REIT scheme buys a fully leased office floor for ₹100 crore, raised from 400 investors putting in ₹25 lakh each. If net rent is ₹9 crore a year and all of it is paid out, each investor receives ₹2.25 lakh a year, a 9% yield.

short: A listed trust that owns cash-earning infrastructure such as toll roads, power lines or pipelines and pays most of that cash to its investors.
kid: Lots of people share their coins to build a road. Every car that drives on it drops a coin in a box, and the box is shared among the people who helped.
detail: An infrastructure investment trust (InvIT) works like a REIT but owns infrastructure: toll and annuity roads, power transmission lines, gas pipelines, telecom towers, fibre networks and similar projects. SEBI's InvIT Regulations of 2014 govern them; under the rules as of 2025 they must distribute at least 90% of net distributable cash flows, and most assets must be completed and earning revenue. IRB InvIT and IndiGrid listed in 2017, and the government has used InvITs such as PowerGrid InvIT and NHAI's National Highways Infra Trust to monetise public assets and recycle capital. Units can be publicly listed or privately placed. The common confusion: InvIT yields often look high because many assets, such as toll concessions, end after a fixed period, so part of each payout is really investors' own capital coming back rather than profit.
example: Say a hypothetical InvIT unit costs ₹100 and pays ₹12 a year, an apparent 12% yield. If ₹5 of that is repayment of capital because its toll-road concession ends in 15 years, only ₹7, or 7%, is income; the rest is your own money being handed back.

short: The yearly cash a property or infrastructure trust pays out per unit, shown as a percentage of the unit's market price.
kid: If a toy box hands you 2 sweets every year and it cost 30 sweets, you can tell how generous it is by comparing the two numbers.
detail: Distribution yield measures the cash a unit-based vehicle, such as a REIT, an InvIT or some funds, pays relative to its price. Distribution per unit (DPU) is the cash paid on each unit over a period, usually the last four quarters (trailing) or the coming year's forecast (forward). Dividing annual DPU by the current unit price gives the yield. Because DPU changes slowly, the yield rises when the unit price falls and falls when the price rises, much like a bond's yield. Investors compare REIT yields with the 10-year G-sec yield to judge whether the extra risk is being paid for. In India, a REIT or InvIT payout can mix interest, dividend and repayment of loans given to its project companies, each taxed differently. The common confusion: distribution yield is not total return, which also includes the change in unit price, and a high yield may include capital being returned.
example: Say a hypothetical REIT paid ₹21 per unit over the last four quarters and trades at ₹300. Its trailing distribution yield is 21 / 300 = 7%. If the price rises to ₹350 with the same payout, the yield drops to 6%.
formula: Distribution yield = Annual distribution per unit / Current unit price x 100

short: A property's yearly rent after running costs, divided by its value; used to compare property deals and to value buildings.
kid: It is like asking: if I pay 10 sweets for this little stall, how many sweets will it give me back each year after I clean and fix it?
detail: The capitalisation rate is net operating income (NOI) divided by a property's current value or purchase price. It is the property market's version of an earnings yield: the yearly income return on the whole building, ignoring any loan and income tax. Turned around, value equals NOI divided by the cap rate, which is how valuers and REIT managers convert rent into a valuation. Cap rates rise when interest rates, vacancy or perceived risk rise, and are lowest for prime, well-let buildings, so a lower cap rate means a pricier property. Because value moves inversely with the cap rate, small changes matter a lot: cap rate compression lifts values and expansion cuts them. The common confusion: the cap rate is not total return or the return on the buyer's own money; it ignores borrowing, rent growth and future price changes.
example: Say a hypothetical office earns NOI of ₹9 crore a year. At a 9% cap rate it is worth ₹9 crore / 0.09 = ₹100 crore. If investors accept a 7.5% cap rate instead, the same income is valued at ₹120 crore, a 20% jump with no change in rent.
formula: Cap rate = Net operating income / Property value x 100; Property value = Net operating income / Cap rate

short: The yearly rent from a property as a percentage of its price; the net version first subtracts costs such as maintenance and property tax.
kid: If you lend your bicycle to a friend and she gives you a few sweets every week, those sweets are what your bicycle earns for you.
detail: Rental yield compares the rent a property earns with what it cost or is worth today. Gross rental yield is annual rent divided by price; net rental yield first deducts costs the owner bears, such as maintenance, property tax, insurance, repairs, brokerage and months when the home stands empty. It is the property cousin of a dividend yield and lets investors compare a flat with a fixed deposit or a REIT. Indian residential rental yields have historically been low, often below home loan interest rates, which is why many buyers count on rising prices rather than rent. Office and warehouse yields are usually higher than housing yields. The common confusion: rental yield is not the full return; total return also includes the change in the property's price, and a home loan changes the return on the buyer's own cash.
example: Say you buy a ₹1 crore flat and rent it out for ₹25,000 a month, or ₹3 lakh a year. Gross rental yield is ₹3 lakh / ₹1 crore = 3%. If maintenance, property tax and empty months cost ₹50,000 a year, net rental yield is ₹2.5 lakh / ₹1 crore = 2.5%.
formula: Gross rental yield = Annual rent / Property price x 100; Net rental yield = (Annual rent - Annual costs) / Property price x 100

short: A property's yearly rent and other income minus the costs of running it, before loan interest, income tax and depreciation.
kid: Your stall gets coins from customers, but you spend some on cups and lemons. What is left after that is what the stall really makes.
detail: Net operating income (NOI) is the core profit measure for income-producing property. It starts with all property revenue, mainly rent plus parking, maintenance recoveries and other charges, and subtracts the costs of operating the building: maintenance, utilities borne by the owner, property tax, insurance and property management. It excludes loan interest and principal, income tax, depreciation and major capital spending, so it shows what the asset earns regardless of how it is financed. NOI is the numerator of the cap rate, the main driver of property valuations and a key line in REIT results, where NOI growth reflects rising rents and occupancy. The common confusion: NOI is not net profit or cash in the owner's pocket; after loan payments and capital spending, the owner's cash can be much lower.
example: Say a hypothetical mall earns ₹12 crore in rent and ₹1 crore from parking and other charges in a year. If maintenance, property tax, insurance and management cost ₹3 crore, NOI is ₹13 crore - ₹3 crore = ₹10 crore. Its ₹4 crore of loan interest is not deducted in NOI.
formula: NOI = Total property revenue - Operating expenses

short: The portion of a building's or market's space, or a hotel's rooms, that is leased or in use; vacancy is the empty remainder.
kid: If a toy house has 10 rooms and dolls live in 9 of them, almost every room is being used. Only one room is empty.
detail: Occupancy rate is the proportion of leasable space, or of rooms in a hotel or beds in a hostel, that is occupied at a date or over a period. Vacancy rate is the mirror image: 100% minus occupancy. For offices and malls, Indian REITs usually report committed occupancy, which counts signed leases even if the tenant has not yet moved in, while physical or economic occupancy counts only space actually used or paying rent. Higher occupancy means more rent, stronger bargaining power with tenants and higher NOI, so investors watch it closely in REIT results and broker reports. Market-wide vacancy also shows whether new supply is outrunning demand. The common confusion: high occupancy alone does not mean strong income; a building can be full because it offered low rents or long rent-free periods.
example: Say a hypothetical office park has 50 lakh sq ft of leasable area, of which 43 lakh sq ft is leased. Occupancy is 43 / 50 = 86% and vacancy is 14%. Leasing another 2 lakh sq ft lifts occupancy to 45 / 50 = 90%.
formula: Occupancy rate = Occupied (leased) area / Total leasable area x 100; Vacancy rate = 100% - Occupancy rate

short: The average time left on a building's leases, weighted by how much rent each tenant pays, showing how secure future rent is.
kid: Some friends promise to keep visiting your stall for a long time and some for a short time. This tells you how long, on average, they will keep coming.
detail: Weighted average lease expiry (WALE) measures how long, on average, a property's or portfolio's income is contracted. Each lease's remaining term is weighted by its share of total rent (sometimes by area) and the results are added up. A longer WALE means rent is locked in for longer, giving visible cash flows that support valuations and borrowing; a short WALE means many leases end soon, bringing re-leasing risk but also a chance to reset rents to market levels. Indian office REITs report WALE alongside occupancy, and investors also study the year-by-year lease expiry schedule. Some reports measure WALE to the first exit or lock-in date rather than final expiry, which gives a shorter figure. The common confusion: WALE is not the building's age or the average original lease length; it is the remaining term.
example: Say a hypothetical building has two tenants: A pays ₹6 crore a year with 8 years left, and B pays ₹4 crore a year with 3 years left. WALE = (6 x 8 + 4 x 3) / (6 + 4) = 60 / 10 = 6 years.
formula: WALE = Sum of (Annual rent of each lease x Remaining lease term) / Total annual rent

short: The floor space in a building that can be rented to tenants, usually measured in square feet, on which rent is charged.
kid: In a big toy house, some rooms are for visitors and some are hallways and stairs everyone shares. The rooms you can lend out to others are what we count here.
detail: Leasable area is the floor space in a commercial building on which tenants pay rent. Definitions vary by market: in Indian office leasing, leasable or chargeable area usually includes the tenant's own space plus a share of common areas such as lobbies and lift areas, while in US shopping centres gross leasable area (GLA) means space tenants occupy exclusively, so the same space can be quoted at different sizes. In India, office and REIT portfolios are usually stated in lakh or million square feet of leasable area, and rent is quoted per sq ft per month. Leasable area drives revenue, occupancy and per-square-foot comparisons across buildings. The common confusion: a building's total construction area, its leasable area and a tenant's usable carpet area are three different numbers, and the gap between them, called loading, directly changes the effective rent.
example: Say a hypothetical office tower has 2 lakh sq ft of leasable area let at ₹100 per sq ft per month. Monthly rent is 2,00,000 x ₹100 = ₹2 crore, or ₹24 crore a year. If tenants' usable carpet area is only 1.5 lakh sq ft, the effective rent on usable space is about ₹133 per sq ft.

short: Top-quality modern office buildings with prime locations, efficient floors, strong services and professional management, which command the highest rents.
kid: Some playhouses are old and creaky, and some are shiny and new with lifts, bright lights and a guard at the gate. The shiny ones are where everyone wants to play.
detail: Grade A office space is the best-quality tier of office buildings. There is no single legal definition; property consultants grade buildings on location and transport links, age and design, large efficient floor plates, ceiling heights, power backup and air conditioning, parking, fire and safety systems, green certifications such as LEED or IGBC, and professional management. Multinationals, global capability centres and large Indian firms prefer Grade A buildings, so these usually enjoy higher rents, higher occupancy and longer leases than Grade B or C buildings. Most assets held by Indian office REITs are Grade A business parks. Investors track Grade A leasing, new supply and vacancy as the main gauge of office demand. The common confusion: Grade A is a market label, not an official certificate, so two consultants may grade the same building differently, and an ageing Grade A building can slip to Grade B.
example: Say a hypothetical Grade A tower leases 1 lakh sq ft at ₹120 per sq ft per month while a nearby Grade B building gets ₹80. The Grade A tower earns ₹1.2 crore a month against ₹80 lakh, a 50% premium for the same floor area.

short: Property used to run businesses and earn rent, such as offices, shops, malls, warehouses, hotels and data centres, rather than homes to live in.
kid: Some buildings are where families sleep and eat. Others are where shops, offices and toy factories do their work, and they pay the owner to use the space.
detail: Commercial real estate (CRE) covers income-producing property used by businesses: offices, malls and high-street shops, warehouses and logistics parks, hotels, data centres and industrial buildings. Owners earn rent under multi-year leases, often with lock-in periods and fixed escalations, so CRE behaves partly like a bond (contracted rent) and partly like equity (rents and values rise and fall with the economy). It is valued mainly on net operating income and cap rates, and tracked through occupancy, absorption and rents. In India, office demand is driven heavily by IT services and global capability centres, and REITs have opened Grade A offices and malls to small investors. CRE loans are also a big exposure for many lenders, notably US regional banks. The common confusion: commercial does not mean only offices, and CRE cycles can differ sharply from the housing cycle.
example: Say a hypothetical warehouse is leased for 9 years at ₹2 crore a year, with rent rising 15% every 3 years. Rent is ₹2 crore a year in years 1-3, ₹2.3 crore in years 4-6 and ₹2.645 crore in years 7-9.

short: Property built for people to live in, such as flats, independent houses, villas and residential plots, whether owner-occupied or rented out.
kid: These are the houses and flats where families live, sleep and play. Some families own their home, and some pay the owner so they can live there.
detail: Residential real estate is property meant for living: apartments, independent houses, villas, row houses and plots for homes. It is the largest asset most households own; an RBI committee in 2017 found that real estate made up about three-quarters of an average Indian household's assets. Demand depends on incomes, jobs, home loan rates, demographics, urbanisation and confidence, while supply depends on land, approvals and developer finances, so prices move in long cycles. Housing matters for the wider economy through construction jobs, demand for cement, steel and paints, bank lending and household wealth. Analysts track sales, launches, unsold inventory, price indices and affordability. In India the market is regulated by RERA and split into primary sales by developers and resale. The common confusion: a rising home price is not cash income; an owner-occupied home is mostly a place to live plus a long-term, often borrowed, bet on prices.
example: Say a family buys an ₹80 lakh flat with ₹16 lakh down and a ₹64 lakh home loan. If the flat's value rises 5% to ₹84 lakh, the ₹4 lakh gain is 25% of their ₹16 lakh down payment, before interest, stamp duty and other costs.

short: Homes priced within reach of low- and middle-income families; in India, defined by size and price limits for tax and lending benefits.
kid: Some houses are so big and fancy that only a few families can get one. Small, simple houses that many more families can manage are what this means.
detail: Affordable housing means homes that low- and middle-income households can buy or rent without spending an unreasonable share of income, often judged by the price-to-income ratio or the share of income going to EMIs. In India it is also a policy category. Under the GST rules as of 2025, a home generally qualifies if its carpet area is up to 60 square metres in the six big metro regions or 90 square metres elsewhere and its value is up to ₹45 lakh; such homes attract 1% GST instead of 5% while under construction. Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana supports the segment with subsidies. Developers face thin margins because urban land is costly, so supply depends on cheap land and incentives. The common confusion: affordable is a defined band in Indian policy, not a loose word for cheap, and affordability also depends on interest rates and incomes, not just price.
example: Under the GST rules as of 2025, a ₹40 lakh under-construction flat that meets the affordable-housing definition attracts 1% GST, or ₹40,000. A ₹50 lakh flat, above the ₹45 lakh cap, attracts 5%, or ₹2.5 lakh.

short: The repeating pattern of boom, oversupply, slump and recovery in property prices, rents and construction, often lasting many years.
kid: Sometimes every child wants a new swing, so lots of swings get built. Then there are too many swings and nobody wants more for a while, until children want swings again.
detail: The real estate cycle describes how property markets swing through recovery, expansion, oversupply and recession. In recovery, vacancies fall and rents firm up; in expansion, rising prices and easy credit encourage new construction; because buildings take years to finish, supply keeps arriving after demand has peaked, creating oversupply; then prices and rents fall until the excess is absorbed. Cycles are long and driven by interest rates, credit availability, incomes, sentiment and construction lags. When prices rise far above what rents and incomes justify, largely on borrowed money, a bubble forms; the US housing bust after 2006 and Japan's land crash of the early 1990s are classic cases. Indian housing went through a long slump from roughly 2014 to 2020 before recovering. The common confusion: property cycles do not move in step with stock markets, and office, retail and housing cycles in different cities can diverge sharply.
example: Say flat prices in a city rise 60% over five years, from ₹1 crore to ₹1.6 crore, then fall 25% as new supply floods in. The price ends at ₹1.2 crore, so a buyer at the peak is down ₹40 lakh while an early buyer is still up 20%.

short: An index that tracks how house prices in a city or country change over time, compared with a base period set to 100.
kid: Imagine writing down every year how many sweets it takes to get a toy house. Looking back at the list shows whether toy houses are getting dearer or cheaper.
detail: A house price index (HPI) measures changes in residential property prices over time, scaled so that a base period equals 100. Because no two homes are identical, index makers adjust for quality: the S&P Case-Shiller indices in the US use a repeat-sales method that compares the same homes sold at different dates, while other indices use hedonic models that price features such as size and location. In India, the RBI publishes a quarterly all-India HPI built from property registration data in ten major cities, and the National Housing Bank publishes RESIDEX for a wider set of cities. Economists use HPIs to track housing wealth, bubbles, affordability and the value of collateral behind home loans. The common confusion: an HPI shows price changes, not price levels, so an index of 180 in one city and 150 in another does not mean the first city is dearer.
example: Say a city's house price index rises from 150 to 162 over a year. Prices rose (162 - 150) / 150 = 8%, so a typical home worth ₹75 lakh a year ago would now be worth about ₹81 lakh.
formula: Price change (%) = (Index this period / Index earlier period - 1) x 100

short: How quickly available homes or office space get sold or leased in a market during a period, showing the strength of demand.
kid: If a toy shop has 12 teddy bears and children take home 3 every week, you can tell how fast the bears are going and when the shelf will be empty.
detail: Absorption measures how fast available supply is taken up by buyers or tenants. In housing, the absorption rate is usually units sold in a period divided by units available, and Indian property consultants also use absorption loosely to mean the number of homes sold in a quarter. For offices, net absorption is the change in occupied space: new space taken up minus space vacated, while gross absorption counts all leasing, including tenants simply moving. A high absorption rate signals a seller's or landlord's market with rising prices or rents; a low rate signals oversupply and discounts. Its inverse gives the months needed to clear current stock. The common confusion: strong leasing or sales headlines can still hide weak net absorption if tenants are only relocating within the city, or if launches are outrunning sales.
example: Say a city has 1,200 unsold flats at the start of a month and 150 are sold during it. The monthly absorption rate is 150 / 1,200 = 12.5%, implying about 8 months to clear the stock if no new projects launch.
formula: Absorption rate = Units sold (or space leased) in a period / Units (or space) available at the start of the period x 100

short: The pile of finished or under-construction homes that remain unsold; an overhang means more homes than buyers are likely to take soon.
kid: If a baker makes 30 cupcakes but only 5 children come each day, many cupcakes sit waiting. Too many waiting cupcakes means the baker should bake fewer.
detail: Unsold inventory is the number of homes launched by developers that have not yet been sold, whether ready or under construction. Analysts express it as months or quarters of inventory: unsold stock divided by the recent average sales rate, which shows how long it would take to clear if no new supply came. An overhang is inventory well above what demand can absorb in a reasonable time. It ties up developers' capital, raises their borrowing, delays new launches and pushes prices down or leads to hidden discounts. Falling months of inventory signals a tightening market where price rises are more likely. In India, consultants track unsold stock in the top seven or eight cities, and the long post-2014 slump was marked by a large overhang. The common confusion: a rising unsold-inventory number can be healthy if launches rise because sales are strong; months of inventory is the better gauge.
example: Say a city has 90,000 unsold homes and sells an average of 6,000 a month. It has 90,000 / 6,000 = 15 months of inventory. If sales rise to 7,500 a month with no new launches, that drops to 12 months.
formula: Months of inventory = Unsold inventory / Average monthly sales

aliases: Real Estate Regulation and Development Act
hl: real estate regulation and development act
short: India's 2016 property law, and the state regulators it created, that make developers register projects, disclose details and deliver homes as promised.
kid: It is like a teacher who checks that whoever is building your playhouse tells the truth, uses your coins only for your playhouse and finishes it on time.
detail: RERA refers to the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, whose main provisions took effect on 1 May 2017, and to the Real Estate Regulatory Authorities each state set up under it. Developers must register projects above small size thresholds before advertising or selling, and disclose approvals, layouts, timelines and carpet areas. Under the Act they must keep 70% of buyers' money in a separate account used only for that project's land and construction, sell on carpet area, fix structural defects reported within five years of possession, and pay interest for delays. Property agents must register too, and disputes go to the authority and then an appellate tribunal. RERA shifted power toward homebuyers and pushed weaker developers out. The common confusion: RERA is enforced by states, so rules and strictness vary across states, and it does not control rents or prices.
example: Say a hypothetical project collects ₹50 crore from flat buyers in a year. Under RERA, at least ₹35 crore (70%) must go into the project's designated bank account and can be withdrawn only in line with construction progress certified by an engineer, an architect and a chartered accountant.

short: An account where a neutral party holds money or documents until agreed conditions are met, then releases them to the right person.
kid: When two friends swap toys, a grown-up holds both toys first. Only when each friend has done what they promised does the grown-up hand the toys over.
detail: An escrow account is a holding arrangement in which a trusted third party, usually a bank or escrow agent, keeps money, securities or documents and releases them only when conditions written into an agreement are met. It protects both sides when they do not fully trust each other. In mergers and acquisitions, part of the price is often held back in escrow to cover warranty or tax claims; in project and infrastructure lending, a borrower's revenues may flow into an escrow account so lenders are paid first; in property deals, a buyer's payment may wait in escrow until title passes; and under RERA, 70% of homebuyers' money must sit in a designated project account, often called the RERA escrow. The common confusion: money in escrow does not yet belong to the receiver, and the agent cannot use it freely; it is not an ordinary account in the receiver's name.
example: Say a buyer pays ₹100 crore for a hypothetical company, with ₹10 crore placed in escrow for 18 months against possible claims. If a ₹3 crore tax demand from before the sale surfaces, the buyer receives ₹3 crore from escrow and the seller gets the remaining ₹7 crore when the period ends.

short: A loan backed by property, usually to buy it; the lender can take and sell the property if the borrower stops paying.
kid: If you borrow a friend's coins to get a toy house, you promise that if you cannot give the coins back, your friend can keep the toy house.
detail: A mortgage is a loan backed by real estate. Strictly, the mortgage is the legal charge that gives the lender a claim over the property until the debt is repaid; in everyday use it means the loan itself. The borrower repays in instalments of interest and principal, usually monthly over 15 to 30 years, and if they default the lender can foreclose, taking and selling the property. In the US, 30-year fixed-rate mortgages dominate and mortgage rates track long-term Treasury yields. In India the same product is usually called a home loan, is mostly floating-rate, with bank loans linked since 2019 to an external benchmark such as the repo rate, and is commonly secured by depositing the title deeds with the lender. Mortgages can be pooled into mortgage-backed securities. The common confusion: the borrower is the mortgagor and the lender is the mortgagee, not the other way round.
example: Say you take a ₹50 lakh mortgage at 9% a year for 20 years. The EMI works out to about ₹44,986 a month; over 240 months you repay about ₹1.08 crore, of which about ₹58 lakh is interest.
formula: EMI = P x r x (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n - 1), where P = loan amount, r = monthly interest rate, n = number of monthly instalments

short: The size of a loan compared with the value of the asset backing it, such as a home, shown as a percentage.
kid: If a toy costs 10 sweets and you borrow 8 from a friend, you pay the other 2 yourself. The more you pay yourself, the safer your friend feels.
detail: The loan-to-value (LTV) ratio divides the loan amount by the assessed value of the asset pledged against it. It is the key safety measure in secured lending: the lower the LTV, the bigger the borrower's own stake and the larger the cushion before a price fall leaves the lender short. Lenders set maximum LTVs. In India the RBI caps LTV on home loans; under the rules as of 2025 the limit is 90% for loans up to ₹30 lakh, 80% for loans above ₹30 lakh and up to ₹75 lakh, and 75% above ₹75 lakh. LTV falls over time as the loan is repaid or the property gains value. Regulators tighten LTV caps to cool housing booms. The common confusion: LTV uses the lender's assessed value, which can be below the price paid, so the buyer may need a bigger down payment than expected.
example: Under the rules as of 2025, a home loan above ₹75 lakh can be at most 75% of the property's value. On a ₹1.2 crore flat, the bank can lend up to ₹90 lakh and the buyer must bring ₹30 lakh, plus stamp duty and registration.
formula: LTV = Loan amount / Assessed value of the property x 100

short: The usable floor area inside a flat's outer walls, including internal walls but excluding balconies, shafts and shared areas like lobbies.
kid: It is the part of your home where you can actually walk, play and put your toys, not the thick outside walls or the stairs everyone shares.
detail: Carpet area is the space a buyer can actually use inside a home. RERA defines it as the net usable floor area of an apartment, excluding the area covered by external walls, service shafts, exclusive balconies or verandahs and exclusive open terraces, but including the area under internal partition walls. Since RERA took effect in 2017, developers must state carpet area and price homes on it, which makes projects comparable and curbed inflated size claims. Before that, flats were usually sold on super built-up area, which adds walls, balconies and a share of lobbies, lifts and clubhouses. Carpet area is also used for affordable-housing eligibility under GST. The common confusion: a price per square foot on super built-up area looks lower than the same home's price on carpet area, so buyers should always compare the carpet-area rate.
example: Say a flat has 800 sq ft of carpet area and 1,040 sq ft of super built-up area, a 30% loading. At ₹10,000 per sq ft of super built-up area it costs ₹1.04 crore, which is really ₹1.04 crore / 800 = ₹13,000 per sq ft of usable carpet area.

short: A flat's carpet area plus its outer walls and balconies; super built-up area also adds a share of lifts, lobbies and other common spaces.
kid: Your room is the floor you play on. Add the walls around it and the hallway and stairs you share with neighbours, and the number gets much bigger.
detail: Built-up area is the carpet area of a flat plus the area under its external walls and spaces such as exclusive balconies. Super built-up area, also called super area or saleable area, goes further and adds a proportionate share of common areas: lobbies, staircases, lift shafts, corridors and sometimes the clubhouse, gym or pool. The gap between super built-up and carpet area is called loading and is usually expressed as a percentage of carpet area; in apartment projects it is commonly around 25-40%. Before RERA, most Indian flats were priced on super built-up area, which let developers quote lower per-square-foot rates. Super area is still widely used in commercial leasing and marketing. The common confusion: a bigger super area does not mean a bigger home; two flats with the same super area can have very different usable space depending on loading.
example: Say a flat has 900 sq ft of carpet area, 1,035 sq ft of built-up area once walls and the balcony are added, and 1,260 sq ft of super built-up area after its share of common areas. Loading is (1,260 - 900) / 900 = 40%.
formula: Loading (%) = (Super built-up area - Carpet area) / Carpet area x 100

short: The ratio of total floor area a builder may construct to the area of the plot, set by city planning rules.
kid: If you have a small patch of sand, a rule says how much castle you may build on it. You can build it wide and short or thin and tall, but not bigger than the rule.
detail: Floor space index (FSI), called floor area ratio (FAR) in many places, is the total built-up floor area allowed on a plot divided by the plot's area. City development control rules fix it by zone, road width and use, and they can allow extra FSI for a premium, through transferable development rights (TDR) or as incentives for redevelopment. FSI decides how much saleable or leasable space a plot can produce, so it is a major driver of land value: higher permitted FSI usually means a pricier plot. Planners raise FSI to add housing supply and limit it to control congestion. Mumbai and other Maharashtra cities use FSI, while Delhi uses FAR, often written as a number like 200 meaning 2.0. The common confusion: FSI is not the number of floors; an FSI of 2 could be two floors covering the whole plot or four floors on half of it.
example: Say a 10,000 sq ft plot has a permitted FSI of 2.5. The builder can construct 10,000 x 2.5 = 25,000 sq ft of floor area. If the city allows premium FSI that raises it to 3.0, buildable area rises to 30,000 sq ft, 20% more space to sell.
formula: FSI = Total built-up floor area / Plot area

short: The minimum value per square foot or square metre that a state government sets for property in an area, used to calculate stamp duty.
kid: The town decides the lowest number of coins a house on each street can be swapped for, so nobody can pretend a big house is worth only a few coins.
detail: The circle rate is the government-notified minimum value of land or built property in a locality, used to calculate stamp duty and registration charges. Names vary: circle rate in Delhi and Uttar Pradesh, ready reckoner rate in Maharashtra, guidance value in Karnataka and guideline value in Tamil Nadu. If a deal is registered below the circle rate, stamp duty is still charged on the circle-rate value. Under the income tax rules as of 2025, if the price is more than 10% below the stamp-duty value, that value is treated as the sale price for the seller's capital gains and the gap may be taxed as the buyer's income. Circle rates aim to curb under-reporting of prices and unaccounted cash. The common confusion: the circle rate is a tax floor, not the market price; actual prices can be well above it, or sometimes below it in weak markets.
example: Say a 1,000 sq ft flat is in an area with a circle rate of ₹8,000 per sq ft, so its circle-rate value is ₹80 lakh. Even if the agreed price is ₹75 lakh, stamp duty at 6% is charged on ₹80 lakh: ₹4.8 lakh instead of ₹4.5 lakh.

short: A tax paid to the state government on legal documents, most notably when a property sale is registered, usually a percentage of its value.
kid: When you get a new toy house, you pay a few extra coins to the town so it writes in its big book that the house is now yours.
detail: Stamp duty is a tax on instruments, the legal documents that record transactions; in India it is levied mainly by states under the Indian Stamp Act and state stamp laws. For property, it is charged on the sale deed, calculated on the higher of the agreed price and the circle-rate value, and must be paid before the document is registered; a separate registration fee goes to the sub-registrar. Rates vary by state and change over time; as of 2025 they typically range from about 4% to 8%, many states charge women buyers less, and registration is often around 1%. Stamp duty also applies to other instruments, such as share transfers, leases and loan agreements. The common confusion: stamp duty is not GST; a buyer of an under-construction flat may pay both, while a ready flat with an occupancy certificate attracts only stamp duty.
example: Say you buy a ₹90 lakh flat in a state charging 6% stamp duty and a 1% registration fee. You pay ₹5.4 lakh in stamp duty and ₹90,000 in registration, a total of ₹6.3 lakh on top of the price.
formula: Stamp duty = Higher of (agreement value, circle-rate value) x Stamp duty rate

short: A contract in which an owner lets someone use a property or other asset for a fixed period in exchange for regular rent.
kid: Your friend lets you play with her doll's house for the whole summer, and you give her a sweet every week. When summer ends, the house goes back to her.
detail: A lease is a contract under which the owner, the lessor, gives a tenant, the lessee, the right to use an asset, usually property but also aircraft, vehicles or machinery, for an agreed term in return for rent. A property lease sets the rent, security deposit, term, lock-in period, escalation, maintenance duties and exit terms. In India, home rentals often use 11-month rent agreements or leave and licence agreements, partly because leases longer than a year must be registered and stamped; office leases commonly run 9 to 15 years with rent stepping up at fixed intervals. For companies, Ind AS 116 and IFRS 16 put most leases on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. The common confusion: the lessor is the owner who receives rent, and the lessee is the user who pays it.
example: Say a hypothetical firm leases 10,000 sq ft of office space at ₹90 per sq ft per month, or ₹9 lakh a month, with a 15% escalation every three years. From year four the rent becomes ₹103.50 per sq ft, or ₹10.35 lakh a month.

short: A deal in which an owner sells an asset, such as a building or aircraft, and immediately rents it back to keep using it.
kid: You give your bicycle to a friend for some coins, then pay her a little each week so you can keep riding it. You get coins now and still have a bike to ride.
detail: In a sale and leaseback, a company sells an asset it uses, typically offices, factories, stores, hospitals or aircraft, to an investor and at the same time signs a long-term lease to keep using it. The seller unlocks cash tied up in property to repay debt or fund growth, while the buyer, often a REIT, insurer or leasing company, gets a long, contracted rent stream. Airlines such as IndiGo have long used aircraft sale and leasebacks. Under Ind AS 116 and IFRS 16, the seller books a right-of-use asset and lease liability and recognises a gain only on the rights actually transferred; if the deal does not qualify as a true sale, it is treated as a loan. The common confusion: a leaseback is not free money; the seller swaps an owned asset for years of rent and gives up any future rise in its value.
example: Say ABC Ltd, a hypothetical company, sells its headquarters for ₹200 crore and leases it back at ₹16 crore a year for 15 years. It gets ₹200 crore of cash today, and the buyer earns an initial yield of 16 / 200 = 8%.

short: Property owned outright with no time limit, unlike leasehold, where you hold the right to use land only for a fixed term.
kid: If a toy is truly yours, you keep it forever. If you can only borrow it until the end of the year, it has to go back one day.
detail: Freehold means owning the land and the building on it outright and indefinitely, free to sell, gift, rent or mortgage it. Leasehold means holding the right to use land or a flat for a fixed term, such as 30, 60 or 99 years, under a lease from the landowner, which in Indian cities is often a development authority such as the DDA, Noida Authority or CIDCO. Leaseholders may pay ground rent, need the lessor's permission or a transfer fee to sell, and must return the property when the lease ends unless it is renewed. Many authorities let owners convert leasehold to freehold for a fee. Buyers and banks value long, clean freehold titles more, so leasehold homes with short remaining terms sell at a discount and are harder to finance. The common confusion: a 99-year lease is not ownership forever; its value falls as the remaining term shrinks.
example: Say a flat sits on land under a 99-year lease that started in 1990. The lease ends in 2089, so a buyer in 2026 gets only 63 remaining years, and a lender may refuse a long loan once fewer years remain than its policy requires.

short: A deal in which a landowner contributes land and a developer builds on it, and they share the finished space or sales revenue.
kid: You have a sandpit and your friend knows how to build great castles. You let them build in your sandpit, and you each keep some of the castles.
detail: A joint development agreement (JDA) lets a developer build a project on land it does not buy. The landowner contributes the land; the developer pays for design, approvals, construction and marketing. In return the landowner gets an agreed share in one of three forms: area sharing, where a fixed share of the finished flats or offices is handed over; revenue sharing, a percentage of sales proceeds; or profit sharing. JDAs are popular in Indian cities such as Bengaluru, Chennai and Hyderabad because they cut the developer's upfront land cost, making growth asset-light, and can earn landowners more than an outright sale. They also bring risks: delays, disputes over shares and approvals, and complex tax treatment, including GST and special capital gains rules. The common confusion: under a JDA the developer usually does not own the land, so a reported land bank that includes JDA land is not all owned outright.
example: Say a landowner signs a JDA for a project with 2 lakh sq ft of saleable area and a 40% area share. The landowner receives 80,000 sq ft of finished space to sell or keep, and the developer keeps 1,20,000 sq ft. Under a 35% revenue share instead, if total sales are ₹500 crore, the landowner gets ₹175 crore.

short: A home or building bought before it is finished and paid for in stages, unlike ready-to-move property, which is complete and can be occupied immediately.
kid: You can pick a toy that is already built and play right away, or pick one still being made, which costs a bit less but means waiting and hoping it gets finished.
detail: Under-construction property is sold before the building is complete. Buyers usually pay through a construction-linked plan, with instalments tied to stages such as the foundation, each slab and possession, and a home loan is released in parts as work progresses. Prices are generally lower than for comparable ready-to-move homes, which are complete, have an occupancy certificate and can be lived in at once. The trade-off is risk: delays, developer insolvency and paying rent plus EMI while waiting. Under the GST rules as of 2025, under-construction homes attract 5% GST, or 1% for affordable housing, while completed homes sold after the occupancy certificate attract none. RERA requires registration before any advertising or booking, so pre-launch offers that take money before registration are a warning sign. The common confusion: a lower headline price does not make an under-construction home cheaper once GST, rent while waiting and delay risk are counted.
example: Say an under-construction flat costs ₹80 lakh plus 5% GST, or ₹84 lakh in total, while a similar ready flat costs ₹88 lakh with no GST. The ₹4 lakh saving disappears if you pay ₹25,000 a month in rent during a 16-month wait, since that rent adds up to ₹4 lakh.

short: The value of new homes or offices a developer has sold during a period, counted when buyers sign up, even though construction is unfinished.
kid: A baker takes orders for birthday cakes that will be baked next month. Counting all the cake orders today shows how busy the bakery will be.
detail: Pre-sales, also called sales bookings, are the value of units a real estate developer has contracted to sell in a period, usually counted when the buyer signs an agreement and pays a booking amount. Listed Indian developers report pre-sales every quarter, along with area sold and average price per square foot, and investors treat them as the main measure of demand and growth. Collections are the cash actually received from buyers in the period, which flows in as construction progresses. Reported revenue is different again: under Ind AS 115, most Indian developers recognise revenue only when a project is completed and handed over, so the income statement can lag bookings by several years. Strong pre-sales with weak collections can signal stretched buyers or slow construction. The common confusion: pre-sales are not revenue or profit, and bookings can be cancelled.
example: Say a hypothetical developer, ABC Realty, books ₹1,000 crore of pre-sales in a year and collects ₹600 crore in cash from buyers. Because only projects handed over count as revenue, it reports revenue of just ₹400 crore, from towers completed this year and sold in earlier years.

short: Land a developer owns or controls for future projects, usually measured in acres or in the square feet it could eventually build.
kid: Before you build sandcastles, you save some patches of sand just for later. The more patches you have, the more castles you can build in future.
detail: A land bank is the land a real estate developer holds for future development, whether bought outright, held through subsidiaries or controlled through joint development agreements. Developers present it in acres and in development potential, the square feet that can be built under the permitted FSI. A large, well-located land bank bought cheaply gives years of project visibility and can support high margins when land values rise. But land locks up capital, earns nothing until developed, carries interest and holding costs, and faces approval, litigation and title risks. Analysts therefore look at land cost per square foot, location, how quickly land is turned into launches, and whether it is owned or under a JDA. The common confusion: a big land bank is not the same as value; land that cannot be approved or sold soon may be worth far less than its size suggests.
example: Say a hypothetical developer holds 50 acres. At 43,560 sq ft per acre that is 21,78,000 sq ft of land, and with a permitted FSI of 2.5 it could build 54,45,000 sq ft, or about 54 lakh sq ft, of space.

short: A hotel's room revenue divided by all the rooms it had available, combining how full it is and the price it charges per room.
kid: Imagine a dollhouse hotel with 10 beds. This number tells you how many coins each bed brought in, counting the empty beds too.
detail: RevPAR, revenue per available room, is the headline performance measure for hotels. It equals room revenue divided by the number of room-nights available, or equivalently occupancy multiplied by the average room rate. The average room rate, called ARR in India and ADR (average daily rate) in the US, is room revenue divided by room-nights actually sold. RevPAR captures both how full a hotel is and how much it charges, so managers can see whether growth comes from pricing or from volume. Listed Indian hotel companies and global chains report RevPAR growth each quarter, and analysts watch it as a gauge of travel demand. It excludes food, beverage and other income, so total revenue per available room (TRevPAR) gives a fuller picture. The common confusion: a higher room rate does not always raise RevPAR; if occupancy falls by more, RevPAR drops.
example: Say a hypothetical 200-room hotel has 6,000 room-nights available in a 30-day month and sells 4,500 of them at an average of ₹8,000. Room revenue is ₹3.6 crore, occupancy is 75%, and RevPAR is ₹3.6 crore / 6,000 = ₹6,000, the same as 75% x ₹8,000.
formula: RevPAR = Room revenue / Room-nights available = Occupancy rate x Average room rate

short: An official document from the local authority confirming a finished building follows approved plans and safety rules and is fit to live in.
kid: Before children can play in a new treehouse, a grown-up checks that it is strong and safe, then gives a sticker that says yes, you may go in.
detail: An occupancy certificate (OC) is issued by the municipal or development authority once a building is complete, after checking that it follows the sanctioned plan and meets norms for structure, fire safety, water, drainage and electricity. It legally permits people to occupy the building. A completion certificate (CC) confirms that construction was finished as per approved plans; in many cities it comes before or alongside the OC, though the terms are sometimes used loosely. Without an OC, residents can struggle to get water and power connections, home loans and resale buyers, and the building can even face demolition orders. Under RERA, developers must obtain these certificates and hand them over. A ready home with an OC also attracts no GST under the rules as of 2025. The common confusion: getting the keys or a possession letter does not mean the building has an OC; buyers should ask for a copy.
example: Under the GST rules as of 2025, a ₹70 lakh flat sold after the occupancy certificate is issued attracts no GST. The same flat sold a month earlier as under-construction would attract 5% GST, or ₹3.5 lakh more.

short: The Indian government's flagship scheme, launched in 2015, that helps poor and middle-income families build or buy homes through grants and loan-interest subsidies.
kid: Some families do not have a safe home. This is a plan where the country helps them build one, by giving them some coins and making it easier to pay back what they borrow.
detail: Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (PMAY) is the central government's Housing for All programme. PMAY-Urban, launched in 2015, supports urban poor and middle-income families through slum redevelopment, affordable housing projects built with partners, direct help for families building their own homes, and the credit-linked subsidy scheme (CLSS), which cut the effective interest on eligible home loans by paying an upfront subsidy into the loan account. PMAY-Gramin, launched in 2016, gives rural households grants to build pucca houses. Crores of homes have been sanctioned, and in 2024 the government approved PMAY-Urban 2.0 for one crore more urban homes, alongside more rural houses. The scheme lifted demand for affordable housing, home loans, cement and steel. Eligibility depends on income and on not already owning a pucca house. The common confusion: PMAY does not give everyone a free home; benefits are targeted, capped and change by phase, so check the current guidelines.
example: Under PMAY-Urban 2.0 as announced in 2024, an eligible family taking a home loan of up to ₹25 lakh on a house worth up to ₹35 lakh can get a 4% interest subsidy on the first ₹8 lakh of the loan. The subsidy is capped at ₹1.80 lakh, paid in five yearly instalments of up to ₹36,000 each.
